title: Plans
goal: Talk about the future — which German does with the present tense — and give reasons with *weil*, the conjunction that sends the verb to the end.
bekal: say goodbye and keep in touch

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Der letzte Kurstag
dialogs.intro: The last day of the course. Everyone is talking about plans — and almost every sentence includes a reason, which means the verb gets sent to the end.

lines.speaker: Frau Weber:
lines.text: Also, das war der letzte Tag. Was machen Sie jetzt?
lines.id: Well, that was the last day. What are you doing now?
lines.literal: so, that was the last day. what do you now?

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Ich mache im September den A2-Kurs. Und dann suche ich einen Job.
lines.id: In September I'm taking the A2 course. And then I'm looking for a job.
lines.literal: I do in-the September the A2-course. and then look-for I a job.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Ich lerne weiter, weil ich die Prüfung bestehen will.
lines.id: I'm going to keep studying, because I want to pass the exam.
lines.literal: I learn further, because I the exam pass want.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ich fliege nächste Woche nach Hause, weil meine Mutter Geburtstag hat.
lines.id: I'm flying home next week, because it's my mother's birthday.
lines.literal: I fly next week home, because my mother birthday has.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.id: Nice! And are you coming back?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja, im Oktober. Ich glaube, dass ich hier bleibe.
lines.id: Yes, in October. I think I'll stay here.
lines.literal: yes, in-the October. I believe, that I here stay.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ich studiere ab Januar hier weiter, weil die Uni gut ist.
lines.id: From January I'm continuing my studies here, because the university is good.
lines.literal: I study from January here further, because the university good is.

lines.speaker: Frau Weber:
lines.text: Das freut mich sehr. Ihr Deutsch ist viel besser geworden.
lines.id: I'm very glad to hear that. Your German has got much better.
lines.literal: that pleases me very. your German is much better become.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Danke. Am Anfang habe ich nichts verstanden.
lines.id: Thank you. At the beginning I didn't understand anything.
lines.literal: thanks. at-the beginning have I nothing understood.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Und jetzt sprichst du besser als ich!
lines.id: And now you speak better than me!
lines.literal: and now speak you better than I!

lines.speaker: Frau Weber:
lines.text: Machen Sie weiter, alle drei. Und bleiben Sie in Kontakt!
lines.id: Keep it up, all three of you. And stay in touch!
lines.literal: make you further, all three. and stay you in contact!

notes: **The future uses the present tense.** *Ich fliege nächste Woche nach Hause* = "I'm flying home next week". There's no special form you have to use; the time phrase makes it clear it hasn't happened yet. English does the same thing — "I'm leaving tomorrow".

***weil* sends the verb to the end.** Compare lines 3 and 9 with an ordinary sentence: *ich **will** die Prüfung bestehen* becomes *…, weil ich die Prüfung bestehen **will***. The conjugated verb moves to the very last position, behind everything — even behind another verb.

***dass* works exactly the same way.** *Ich glaube, **dass** ich hier **bleibe***. This conjunction is used after verbs like *glauben* (believe), *denken* (think), *hoffen* (hope), *wissen* (know), *sagen* (say).

**The comma is required.** A clause with *weil* or *dass* is **always** preceded by a comma in German. It isn't a style choice as it is in English — here the comma marks a boundary in the sentence structure.
**Line 10: *ist … geworden*.** The Perfekt of *werden* (to become), using *sein*. A change of state — exactly the group you put in place in unit 18.

***Das freut mich*** ("that pleases me") is how you say you're glad about good news. Its cousin from introductions: *Freut mich* — which you've been using since unit 1, and now you know where it comes from.

grammars.title: Talking about the future
body: German has an official future tense with *werden*, but in everyday conversation it's rarely used for plans. What people use is the present tense plus a time phrase.

head: How
Example
When it's used
rows: a definite plan — the most common way
Was hast du am Wochenende vor?

after: The time phrases used most often for the future: *morgen*, *übermorgen*, *nächste Woche*, *nächsten Monat*, *nächstes Jahr*, *bald* (soon), *in zwei Tagen*, *ab Januar*.

You need to **recognize** *werden* + infinitive when you hear it, but you don't need to use it yet. At A1, *Ich fahre morgen* is completely enough — and actually sounds more natural than *Ich werde morgen fahren*.

grammars.title: weil and dass — verb to the end
body: Up to unit 16 you used conjunctions that don't change the word order (*und*, *aber*, *oder*, *denn*). *Weil* and *dass* belong to the other group: both create a **subordinate clause**, and in a subordinate clause the conjugated verb moves to the last position.
after: The second row shows what confuses people most: if there's a modal verb, **the modal is what moves to the end**, and the main verb stands right in front of it. *…, weil ich die Prüfung **bestehen will***. The order is the reverse of an ordinary sentence.

The subordinate clause can also come **first**, and then it counts as the first element — so the verb of the main clause follows immediately: *Weil es regnet, **bleibe** ich zu Hause.* Two verbs meet in the middle of the sentence, separated by a comma. This order sounds very German, and using it even once lifts your German up a level.
To answer *Warum?* in quick conversation, people often just reply with *Weil…*: *Warum lernst du Deutsch?* — *Weil ich in Deutschland arbeiten will.*

head: German
English

What are your plans for next year?
I'd like to work in Germany.
I want to take the exam.
Ich mache im September den A2-Kurs.
In September I'm taking the A2 course.
Ich hoffe, dass wir uns wiedersehen.
I hope we'll see each other again.
Ich denke, dass Deutsch schwer ist.

head: Question
Answer with weil
rows: Weil ich in Deutschland arbeiten will.

blocks.text: Look at row four: in a subordinate clause, the past tense puts the **helper verb** at the end, after the Partizip II. *…, weil ich nicht **geschlafen habe**.* Once again the order is the reverse of an ordinary sentence — and once again there's only one rule: the conjugated verb goes to the end.
This book ends here, so it's fitting to close with the sentences people use to end a conversation — and to make sure the conversation continues.

blocks.title: A closing exercise for yourself
items: Write five sentences about your plans for the next six months, each with a reason using *weil*.
Read them out loud. If all five come out without long pauses, you've reached A1 — not A1 on paper, but A1 that comes out of your mouth.
Keep what you wrote. Six months from now, rewrite it in the past tense using the *Perfekt*, then compare the two. It's the best way to see how far you've come.

blocks.text: *Vielen Dank fürs Mitmachen — und alles Gute für Ihren Weg mit der deutschen Sprache!*
